   "tldr": "Across one college-age football season, blood levels of the candidate CTE markers did not change significantly. Phosphorylated tau was higher in players than controls, but the study is too small to show what this means.",

    ABSTRACT                                                                                                              ARTICLE HISTORY
    This study measured the relationship between head-injury exposure and later-in-life cognitive and                     Received 2 April 2024
    emotional symptoms in aging collegiate football players who participated in the College Level                         Accepted 2 May 2024
    Aging Athlete Study. Linear regressions examined the relationship between various head-injury                         KEYWORDS
    exposure variables (head-injury exposure estimate [HIEE], number of diagnosed concussions, and                        Amateur sports;
    symptomatic hits to the head) and subjective cognitive function, objective cognitive function, and                    concussions; cognitive
    emotional/mood symptoms. Additional regressions evaluated the impact of emotional symptoms                            decline; repetitive
    on subjective cognitive decline and objective cognitive function. Participants (n = 216) were                         head-injury
    50–87 years old (M = 63.4 [8.5]), 91% White, and well-educated (bachelor’s/graduate degree =
    92%). HIEE did not predict scores on cognitive or emotional/mood symptom measures (p’s > .169).
    Diagnosed concussions had a small effect on depression symptoms (p = .002, b = 0.501, R2 = .052)
    and subjective cognitive symptoms (p = .002, b = 0.383, R2 = .051). An emotional symptom index
    had a stronger relationship (p < .001, b = 0.693, R2 = .362) with subjective cognitive functioning
    but no significant relationship with objective cognitive function (p = .052, b = −0.211, R2 = .020).
    Controlling for emotional symptoms, the relationship between concussions and subjective
    cognitive symptoms was attenuated (p = .078, R2 = .011). Findings suggested that head-injury
    exposure was not significantly related to cognitive or emotional/mood outcomes in former
    collegiate football players and highlighted the importance of current emotional/mood symptoms
    on subjective cognitive function.

 "primaryDomain": "Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains": ["Brain Health & Psychology"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Research & Analytics"],
 "sports": ["American Football"],
 "populations": ["Male Athletes", "Collegiate"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Survey and telephone cognitive screening study of 216 former male collegiate football players aged 50 to 87 years in the CLEAATS study. Hierarchical regressions, adjusted for age and education, related three head-injury exposure measures (a cumulative head-injury exposure index, self-reported diagnosed concussions, and symptomatic hits) to subjective cognitive complaints, objective cognitive screening (TICS-m), and depression, anxiety and emotional dysregulation. The exposure index did not predict any outcome. Diagnosed concussions were associated with small increases in depressive symptoms and subjective cognitive complaints, and an emotional symptom index was strongly associated with subjective complaints (R2 = 0.36) but not with the objective screening score.",
 "screeningLimitations": "This is a single cross-sectional survey in a homogeneous, well-educated, mostly White sample, with self-reported concussions and retrospective exposure recall. The authors note reverse causation is possible, the cognitive measure was a brief telephone screen, and the effects are small.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the emotional-symptom link as proof that concussion does not affect thinking, when the study measured one time point with a brief screen and cannot rule out other causes or reverse causation.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2024,
   "citation": "Schaffert, J., Datoc, A., Sanders, G. D., Didehbani, N., LoBue, C., & Cullum, C. M. Repetitive head-injury exposure and later-in-life cognitive and emotional outcomes among former collegiate football players: a CLEAATS investigation. International Review of Psychiatry. 2024;36(3):233–242.",
   "doi": "10.1080/09540261.2024.2352572",
   "abstract": "The authors examined how head-injury exposure measures relate to later-life subjective and objective cognition and emotional symptoms in 216 former collegiate football players aged 50 to 87. The cumulative exposure index did not predict any outcome. Diagnosed concussions had small associations with depression and subjective cognitive symptoms, and emotional symptoms were strongly associated with subjective cognitive complaints.",
   "tldr": "In older former college players, cumulative head-injury exposure did not predict cognition or mood. Current mood symptoms were strongly linked to self-reported memory and thinking complaints, so mood should be considered when a former player reports cognitive problems.",
   "methods": "Former male collegiate football players (n = 216, aged 50 to 87) from the CLEAATS study completed a survey on playing history, diagnosed concussions and symptomatic hits, and a head-injury exposure index was calculated from high school and college contact practice, games and position. Subjective cognition was measured with the Cognitive Functioning Instrument (CFI), objective cognition with the modified Telephone Interview for Cognitive Status (TICS-m, n = 157), and mood with the PHQ-8, GAD-7 and NQoL Emotional and Behavioral Dyscontrol scale. Hierarchical linear regressions were adjusted for age and education, and a p < .01 threshold was used.",
   "findings": "The head-injury exposure index did not predict TICS-m, CFI, PHQ-8, GAD-7 or NQoL EBD (all p > .169). Each diagnosed concussion was associated with a small increase in PHQ-8 depressive symptoms (b = 0.50, p = .002, R2 change 0.052) and CFI subjective cognitive symptoms (b = 0.38, p = .002, R2 change 0.051). The emotional index was strongly associated with CFI scores (b = 0.69, p < .001, R2 = 0.36) but not with TICS-m scores (p = .052). When emotional symptoms were controlled, the concussion and CFI association was no longer significant (p = .078). Symptomatic hits were associated only with the NQoL EBD measure of emotional dysregulation (p = .006, R2 change 0.042).",
   "limitations": "The design is cross-sectional and survey-based, so reverse causation is possible, as the authors note, since depression may increase reports of past concussions and symptoms. Concussion history and playing exposure are self-reported and recalled. The sample is male, well-educated and mostly White, and the cognitive measure was a brief telephone screen rather than full neuropsychological testing. Some analyses had missing data, and the authors describe the effects as small. The mean age is given as 63.4 in the abstract and 64.1 in the Results and Table 2, so the value is not settled in the text.",
   "practicalImplications": "Self-reported subjective cognitive complaints in former players were strongly linked to current mood symptoms and only weakly to objective screening scores. Clinicians assessing a former player's cognitive complaints should consider current mood symptoms and objective testing, and should not rely on self-report alone. Head-injury exposure measures did not predict later cognition or mood in this group, so exposure history alone should not be used to predict later-life outcomes.",
   "athleteDev": "This study does not inform performance training. Its participants were former collegiate players aged 50 and older, and none of its measures concerned current training, load or performance.",
   "rtp": "This study cannot inform return to sport. It did not assess current injury, rehabilitation or return-to-play decisions, and its concussion results concern long-term symptoms and mood in retired players, which should not be applied to a current athlete's return decision."
 }
}
